Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The former Halliburton subsidiary KBR has been charged with bribing Nigerian government officials with "tens of millions of dollars" to obtain "billions of dollars in contracts," according to court documents filed late Friday in Houston, Texas. KBR was spun off from its former parent corporation Halliburton in 2007. Justice Department lawyers filed an "information," which is generally associated with an expected plea agreement. The Justice Department had no comment on the filing, but officials familiar with the case said they expected KBR representatives to appear Wednesday in federal court in Houston. The 22-page court document outlines a complex joint venture involving KBR and the Nigeria government-owned National Petroleum Corporation charged with developing the country's oil and gas industry. The contracts involved the design and construction of a natural gas plant. The government documents say the joint venture included payments to international consultants to bribe Nigerian officials. The alleged violations of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act come after the conviction of Albert Stanley, KBR's former chief executive officer, who pleaded guilty to bribery last fall. "We are not providing comment at this time," said company spokeswoman Heather Browne in an e-mail. She referred CNN to a filing in October that cited a consortium that included KBR called TSKJ. It said, "information has been uncovered suggesting that, commencing at least 10 years ago, members of TSKJ planned payments to Nigerian officials. We have reason to believe, based on the ongoing investigations, that payments may have been made by agents of TSKJ to Nigerian officials. "The government has recently confirmed that it has evidence of such payments. The government has also recently advised Halliburton and KBR that it has evidence of payments to Nigerian officials by another agent in connection with a separate KBR-managed offshore project in Nigeria and possibly evidence of payments in connection with other projects in Nigeria." The company said that in June 2004 it terminated its relationship with Stanley, and noted his guilty plea. "By the plea, Mr. Stanley admitted that he participated in a scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials and that payments were made by agents of TSKJ to Nigerian officials in connection with the construction and expansion by TSKJ of the complex at Bonny Island," it said. KBR, which was spun off from its former parent corporation Halliburton in 2007, has been under fire for its business practices in providing logistical support to the U.S. war effort in Iraq. The Nigerian charges are separate from KBR's contracts in Iraq and Kuwait. CNN Justice Producer Terry Frieden contributed to this story.

**Justice Department charges KBR in Nigerian bribery scheme tied to natural gas contracts**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Justice Department charged engineering and construction firm KBR Inc. in connection with a long-running scheme to bribe Nigerian government officials in order to win contracts to build liquefied natural gas facilities, federal officials said.

KBR, formerly a subsidiary of Halliburton Co., was accused of participating in a conspiracy to pay tens of millions of dollars in bribes to Nigerian officials to secure engineering, procurement and construction contracts for a natural gas plant on Bonny Island, Nigeria. The contracts were worth billions of dollars, according to prosecutors.

The case centered on the company’s role in a four-company joint venture that sought and obtained contracts to build and expand Nigeria LNG Ltd.’s liquefied natural gas complex. Authorities said the bribes were routed through consultants and intermediaries in an effort to influence Nigerian officials and obtain business.

Federal prosecutors brought the case under the **Foreign Corrupt Practices Act**, the U.S. law that prohibits companies and individuals from bribing foreign officials to win or retain business. The law also requires publicly traded companies to keep accurate books and records and maintain internal controls.

A key figure in the investigation was **Albert “Jack” Stanley**, a former KBR chairman and chief executive. Stanley previously pleaded guilty to charges related to the bribery scheme, admitting that he helped arrange improper payments to Nigerian officials while KBR was still part of Halliburton. Prosecutors said Stanley and others used sham consulting agreements to disguise the payments.

Halliburton, which spun off KBR in 2007, was also drawn into the matter because KBR operated as its engineering and construction unit during much of the period covered by the allegations. U.S. authorities said the misconduct occurred before KBR became an independent company.

The Justice Department said the bribery scheme lasted for years and involved payments intended to influence the award of contracts for the Bonny Island project, one of the largest natural gas infrastructure developments in Africa.

KBR agreed to resolve the criminal case by pleading guilty and paying a substantial criminal penalty. In a related civil settlement, U.S. securities regulators also pursued penalties and disgorgement tied to the same conduct.

The case became one of the most significant U.S. foreign bribery prosecutions of its time, underscoring the Justice Department’s increased use of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act against major corporations accused of corrupt practices overseas.

**DOJ Filing Targets KBR Over Alleged Bribery Scheme Tied to Nigerian LNG Project**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*[Dateline]*

The U.S. Department of Justice has filed new court papers alleging that KBR Inc. bears responsibility for a long-running bribery scheme connected to multibillion-dollar contracts to build liquefied natural gas facilities on Bonny Island, Nigeria — a case that has drawn in former Halliburton executives, an international construction consortium known as TSKJ, and one of the most prominent foreign-bribery prosecutions in recent U.S. history.

In the filing, prosecutors describe what they say was a coordinated effort by companies in the TSKJ joint venture to secure engineering, procurement and construction contracts from Nigeria LNG Ltd. by funneling payments to Nigerian government officials. The contracts, awarded over several years, were tied to the development and expansion of the Bonny Island LNG complex, one of Africa’s largest energy infrastructure projects.

KBR, formerly a Halliburton subsidiary, was a member of TSKJ, a four-company consortium whose name came from its participants: Technip of France, Snamprogetti of Italy, Japan’s JGC Corp., and Kellogg Brown & Root, then part of Halliburton. Prosecutors have long alleged that the consortium used intermediaries and consulting agreements to channel improper payments to Nigerian officials in exchange for help obtaining contracts valued in the billions of dollars.

The DOJ’s filing relies in part on the guilty plea of Albert “Jack” Stanley, KBR’s former chairman and chief executive, who admitted to participating in a conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Stanley, who also served as a senior Halliburton executive, pleaded guilty in 2008 to charges that he helped arrange bribes to Nigerian officials to win work for TSKJ on the Bonny Island project.

According to prosecutors, Stanley and others met repeatedly to discuss the use of consultants to make payments to Nigerian officials. The government has alleged that the consortium retained agents to help route the payments, including through agreements that appeared on paper to be for legitimate services. Stanley admitted that the scheme involved tens of millions of dollars in intended bribe payments and that the purpose was to secure favorable treatment for TSKJ in the awarding of LNG contracts.

The DOJ filing argues that KBR cannot distance itself from the conduct because its executives and employees allegedly participated in or benefited from the arrangement while the company was part of Halliburton. Prosecutors contend that the bribery scheme was not a rogue act by a single executive but part of a broader effort to obtain lucrative contracts for the joint venture.

KBR has previously faced scrutiny from U.S. and international authorities over the Bonny Island project. The company and Halliburton have maintained at various points that they cooperated with investigators and addressed compliance issues after the conduct came to light. Any current response from KBR to the latest filing was not immediately available.

The Bonny Island investigation became one of the landmark cases under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the U.S. anti-bribery law that prohibits companies and individuals from paying foreign officials to obtain or retain business. The matter attracted attention not only because of the size of the alleged payments but also because of the stature of the companies involved and the global nature of the alleged scheme.

At the center of the allegations is Nigeria LNG Ltd., a company formed to develop and operate LNG facilities in Nigeria. The Bonny Island plant was built in stages, often referred to as “trains,” with each expansion representing major new contract opportunities for engineering and construction firms. Prosecutors have alleged that TSKJ sought to influence the award of several of those contracts by paying or promising bribes to Nigerian officials with authority or influence over the project.

Stanley’s guilty plea marked a major turning point in the investigation. In court, he admitted that he and others arranged for consultants to be hired with the understanding that portions of their fees would be used to bribe Nigerian officials. The plea implicated senior-level decision-making and provided prosecutors with a key insider account of how the alleged scheme operated.

The DOJ’s latest filing underscores the government’s position that companies can be held accountable for misconduct carried out through joint ventures, subsidiaries, agents and intermediaries — a recurring theme in FCPA enforcement. Prosecutors have increasingly focused on whether companies used third parties to conceal improper payments while continuing to profit from contracts obtained through corrupt means.

Legal analysts say the case remains significant because it illustrates the risks multinational companies face when participating in large overseas infrastructure projects, particularly in sectors such as energy, defense and construction where government approvals and state-owned enterprises often play central roles.

The filing also revives attention on Halliburton’s historical connection to the matter. KBR operated for decades as Halliburton’s engineering and construction arm before being spun off as a separate public company. Stanley held leadership roles during the period when the alleged conduct occurred, and prosecutors have said the scheme overlapped with KBR’s years under Halliburton ownership.

The DOJ has not alleged that every employee of KBR or Halliburton was aware of the bribery arrangement. But its filing maintains that the company, through senior officials and representatives, was involved in the conspiracy and benefited from contracts obtained by TSKJ.

The case is part of a broader wave of enforcement actions arising from the Bonny Island project. Authorities in multiple countries have examined the conduct of TSKJ members and related agents. U.S. prosecutors have used the matter to emphasize that anti-corruption enforcement can reach foreign companies, U.S. issuers, former executives and joint-venture partners when transactions touch U.S. markets, banking channels or corporate entities.

For KBR, the filing adds to the legal fallout from conduct that allegedly occurred years before the company completed its separation from Halliburton. For the DOJ, it represents another effort to establish accountability in a bribery scandal that prosecutors say helped steer some of the world’s most valuable energy contracts.

The court will now consider the DOJ’s arguments as the case proceeds. No final determination of liability has been made in the latest filing, and KBR is expected to contest any allegations it disputes.
